metadata.title: IR band map for CO2 hydrogenation
metadata.description: Approximate band positions for surface and gas-phase species in CO₂ hydrogenation. Exact positions depend on support, coverage, and reaction conditions. The asterisk (*) denotes a surface-bound species.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ asymmetric stretch (νₐₛ) — R-branch envelope maximum at ~2360 cm⁻¹, paired with the P-branch at ~2335. The Q-branch between them is symmetry-forbidden — see co2_asym_2349_Q. Saturates at high pCO₂.

references.note: νₐₛ band origin (00011←00001) at 2349 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); 2360 here is the R-branch envelope maximum, not a single measured line.
Gas-phase CO₂ R-branch observed at 2373 cm⁻¹ during DRM at 600°C (Table 3); reactant concentration marker.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ asymmetric stretch (νₐₛ) — Q-branch at the 2349 cm⁻¹ band origin. Forbidden by symmetry for this Σᵤ⁺←Σg⁺ parallel transition, so no rotational line actually appears here; marks the gap between the R- and P-branch envelopes.

references.note: νₐₛ band origin (00011←00001) at 2349 cm⁻¹ (Table 2) — the forbidden Q-branch position itself, not an observed line.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ asymmetric stretch (νₐₛ) — P-branch envelope maximum at ~2335 cm⁻¹, paired with the R-branch at ~2360. Same forbidden-Q gap as the R-branch entry — see co2_asym_2349_Q. Saturates at high pCO₂.

references.note: νₐₛ band origin (00011←00001) at 2349 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); 2335 here is the P-branch envelope maximum, not a single measured line.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (δ) — R-branch (ΔJ = +1) at ~700 cm⁻¹. Higher-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the P-branch at ~660. Q-branch is allowed (Σ→Π transition) and appears as a sharp spike at ~667 between P and R envelopes.

references.note: Reports the δ band origin (01101←00001) at 667 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); ~700 here is the R-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (δ) — Q-branch (ΔJ = 0) at ~667 cm⁻¹. Sharp, intense spike between P and R envelopes; allowed because this mode is a Σ→Π (perpendicular) transition. Saturates very quickly at modest pCO₂.

references.note: Q-branch coincides with the reported δ band origin (01101←00001) at 667 cm⁻¹ (Table 2) — the fundamental bending mode.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (δ) — P-branch (ΔJ = −1) at ~660 cm⁻¹. Lower-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~700. Atmospheric CO₂ in the beam path contributes to this region; routinely seen even with good purging.

references.note: Reports the δ band origin (01101←00001) at 667 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); ~660 here is the P-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3730 cm⁻¹; (νₛ + νₐₛ) R-branch — upper Fermi-resonance component, R-side. Useful for high-pressure quantification when the νₐₛ fundamental saturates. Genuinely Fermi-coupled to the 2δ+νₐₛ doublet below (~3600 cm⁻¹), not just two coincidentally nearby combination bands — see co2_sym_1388 for why the resonance between νₛ and 2δ carries through into both bands' own +νₐₛ combination levels.

references.note: Reports the νₛ+νₐₛ band origin (10011←00001) at ~3715 cm⁻¹ (Table 2, upper Fermi-resonance pair); ~3730 here is the R-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3699 cm⁻¹; (νₛ + νₐₛ) P-branch — upper Fermi-resonance component, P-side. P/R-branch separation ~30 cm⁻¹; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~3730. See co2_sym_1388 for why this combination doublet is genuinely Fermi-coupled to the 2δ+νₐₛ one below, not just nearby.

references.note: Reports the νₛ+νₐₛ band origin (10011←00001) at ~3715 cm⁻¹ (Table 2, upper Fermi-resonance pair); ~3699 here is the P-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3627 cm⁻¹; (2δ + νₐₛ) R-branch — lower Fermi-resonance component, R-side. Separation between Fermi pair (3730 vs 3627) ~107 cm⁻¹ is fixed. See co2_bend_overtone_1285 for why this combination doublet is genuinely Fermi-coupled to the νₛ+νₐₛ one above, not just nearby.

references.note: Reports the 2δ+νₐₛ band origin (10012←00001) at ~3613 cm⁻¹ (Table 2, lower Fermi-resonance pair); ~3627 here is the R-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3597 cm⁻¹; (2δ + νₐₛ) P-branch — lower Fermi-resonance component, P-side. P/R-branch separation ~30 cm⁻¹; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~3627. See co2_bend_overtone_1285 for why this combination doublet is genuinely Fermi-coupled to the νₛ+νₐₛ one above, not just nearby.

references.note: Reports the 2δ+νₐₛ band origin (10012←00001) at ~3613 cm⁻¹ (Table 2, lower Fermi-resonance pair); ~3597 here is the P-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~2077 cm⁻¹: one quantum of the (IR-forbidden) symmetric stretch ν₁ plus one quantum of the bend ν₂ — the combined state has Πu symmetry, which is dipole-allowed even though ν₁ alone isn't. The most intense combination band in the 2200–1900 cm⁻¹ region. Falls squarely in the linear metal-CO stretching range, so in a DRIFTS/transmission cell with gas-phase CO₂ present it's a recurring misassignment risk against a genuine surface ν(CO) band at the same position. Intensity grows with CO₂ pressure and temperature, not with anything happening at the catalyst surface — a useful discriminator. Always check for this band before assigning a 2077 cm⁻¹ feature to surface CO.

references.note: Table 3, band J: very strong, narrow Q-branch, ν₁+ν₂ (11101←00001, ¹²C¹⁶O₂) — most intense combination band in the investigated range; used as the intensity-normalization reference (no temperature dependence). Particularly pronounced in their long-path-length Praying Mantis HTRC cell; intensity amplified at elevated CO₂ pressures.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ symmetric stretch (νₛ) band origin at ~1388 cm⁻¹. Strictly IR-forbidden by symmetry (Σg⁺ — centrosymmetric, no dipole moment change); observed only in Raman spectroscopy. Listed here as the explicit parent mode for the νₛ+νₐₛ combination band (~3715 cm⁻¹) and as the Fermi-resonance partner of 2δ (see co2_bend_overtone_1285) — the same cubic anharmonic term (coupling q₁ and q₂² directly) that mixes this pair also mixes their +νₐₛ combination levels above, since that term doesn't involve q₃ at all; that's why the νₛ+νₐₛ / 2δ+νₐₛ combination doublets further up are themselves marked as a Fermi-resonance pair too — same underlying coupling, carried up by one shared νₐₛ quantum on each side.

references.note: νₛ band origin (Table 2); IR-inactive (Σg⁺) — included for context as the Fermi-dyad partner of 2δ and parent of the νₛ+νₐₛ combination band.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending overtone (2δ, the l=0 / Σg⁺ component of two bending quanta) at ~1285 cm⁻¹ — like νₛ, strictly IR-forbidden by symmetry; observed only in Raman spectroscopy. In genuine Fermi resonance with νₛ (~1388 cm⁻¹, see co2_sym_1388): the cubic anharmonic coupling between them pushes both away from their naive, uncoupled positions (~1334 and ~1388) to the observed ~1285/1388 split. The same coupling carries through into the νₛ+νₐₛ / 2δ+νₐₛ combination bands further up (~3700/3600 cm⁻¹), which is why those two combination doublets are themselves marked as a Fermi-resonance pair.

references.note: 2δ (l=0) band origin (Table 2); IR-inactive (Σg⁺) — the Raman-observed, Fermi-resonance-shifted position, well below the naive uncoupled estimate of ~1334 cm⁻¹ (2×667).

bands.description: Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — R-branch (ΔJ = +1) at ~2170 cm⁻¹. Higher-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the P-branch at ~2115. Q-branch forbidden for diatomic CO (Σ→Σ transition), leaving a characteristic gap at ~2143 cm⁻¹ between R and P branches — see co_stretch_2143_Q.

references.note: R-branch of CO rotovibrational spectrum clearly visible at 2176 cm⁻¹ (Figs. 4–6). Band shape and width are temperature-dependent: higher T broadens the envelope via Maxwell–Boltzmann redistribution of rotational populations. Accurate gas-phase subtraction requires a SiC reference spectrum collected under identical gas composition and temperature.

bands.description: Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — Q-branch at the ~2143 cm⁻¹ band origin. Forbidden by symmetry for this Σ→Σ transition, so no rotational line actually appears here; marks the gap between the R- and P-branch envelopes.

references.note: The forbidden Q-branch position sits at the CO fundamental band origin (~2143 cm⁻¹), consistent with the midpoint of their observed P (2114 cm⁻¹) and R (2176 cm⁻¹) branch maxima (Fig. 4).

bands.description: Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — P-branch (ΔJ = −1) at ~2115 cm⁻¹. Lower-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~2170. P/R splitting ~55 cm⁻¹ at room temperature; envelope broadens and shifts intensity to higher-J lines as temperature increases (Maxwell–Boltzmann redistribution). Same forbidden-Q gap as the R-branch entry — see co_stretch_2143_Q.

references.note: P-branch of CO rotovibrational spectrum at 2114 cm⁻¹ (Fig. 4). P/R splitting ~62 cm⁻¹ (2176−2114 cm⁻¹). Temperature-dependent lineshape; imperfect background correction using a SiC reference at the wrong temperature leaves a spurious positive artefact near 2220 cm⁻¹ (Fig. 5d–e).

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric C-H stretch (νₐₛ, T₂ mode); sharp Q-branch at ~3019 cm⁻¹ with rotational P/R structure.

references.note: Table 3: νₛ(–CH₃) at 3016 cm⁻¹; gas-phase CH₄ C-H stretch during DRM at 600°C over Ni-Ce-Fe/La-Al₂O₃.

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric bending (δₐₛ, T₂ mode) at ~1306 cm⁻¹.

references.note: Table 3: ν(CH₄, Gaseous) at 1306 cm⁻¹; present across all catalysts under DRM at 600°C; gas-phase CH₄ concentration marker.

bands.description: Gas methane symmetric bending (δₛ, E mode) at ~1534 cm⁻¹. IR-forbidden by symmetry (E in Td — no T₂ component); observed only in Raman spectroscopy. Listed here as the explicit parent mode for the δₛ+νₐₛ combination band (~4220 cm⁻¹).
Gas methane symmetric C-H stretch (νₛ, A₁ mode) at ~2917 cm⁻¹. IR-forbidden by symmetry (A₁ in Td has no T₂/dipole component); observed only in Raman spectroscopy.

references.note: Recommended experimental value 0.362 eV (≈2920 cm⁻¹) for ν₁, A₁ symmetric stretch, Raman-active/IR-inactive; calculated value 0.390 eV (≈3146 cm⁻¹) given alongside it in the same table.

bands.description: Gas methane combination band at ~4220 cm⁻¹; useful for high-pressure quantification when νₐₛ saturates. Often outside standard DRIFTS window.

Linear (atop) CO bonded end-on to a single metal atom — the most common single-center coordination geometry for adsorbed CO, and usually the strongest, sharpest band in a CO-probe spectrum. Frequency depends on metal identity, oxidation state, coordination environment, and surface coverage, all acting through their effect on metal→CO π-backdonation: more backdonation into the CO 2π* orbital weakens and red-shifts the C-O bond, electron-poor or partially oxidized sites push it the other way. ¹³CO substitution red-shifts this band by several tens of cm⁻¹ from the ¹²CO position, a standard isotope-labeling check for confirming a feature is genuinely a CO stretch and not a coincidentally overlapping species.

references.note: Three linear Cu⁰-CO components (Fig. 3a; −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum); the 2065/2030 cm⁻¹ pair (very unsaturated centers) loses intensity with Ga loading, attributed to Ga₂O₃ diffusing to the Cu particle edge.

Linear (on-top) CO on metallic Co at 2041 cm⁻¹ (Fig. 5a, Section 3.3). 14% Co/Siralox shows cobalt carbonyl signal spanning 2100–1700 cm⁻¹ with maximum at ~2059 cm⁻¹ (Fig. 4c, Section 3.2). Gas-phase CO R/P branches at 2176/2114 cm⁻¹ are simultaneously visible and must be subtracted; ill-resolved bridged/multibonded CO bands appear below 2000 cm⁻¹.

Linear ¹²CO on Pt at the Pt–CeO₂ interface at 2053 cm⁻¹ (Fig. 4a); red-shifted by ~20–30 cm⁻¹ from bare Pt (2070–2080 cm⁻¹) due to enhanced π-backdonation from highly reduced CeO₂. SSITKA confirms this species is an active intermediate in RWGS: isotopic exchange rate matches CO(g) production rate. The ¹³C-substituted counterpart is filed separately — see ν(¹³CO) linear (μ₁).

On-top (linear, μ₁) CO on Pd nanoparticles typically observed at 2080–2090 cm⁻¹ (Introduction, citing prior SFG work), distinct from this same paper's own focus on bridge-site coverage dependence (see co_bridge_mu2_1900).

Fig. 7a, and Figs. S18/S19 in the SI (MCR-resolved, He+CO₂ vs H₂+He switching, 230 °C, 20 bar): CO* on metallic Cu at 2113 cm⁻¹ (Cu–Zn/SiO₂), 2115 cm⁻¹ (Cu/SiO₂) and 2108 cm⁻¹ (Cu–In/SiO₂), produced in situ by decomposition of κ²-HCOO*(Cu) rather than dosed — its rise mirrors the formate component's decay, making it the spectroscopic signature of the unselective RWGS branch. Invisible at steady state on every catalyst (it is hydrogenated away as fast as it forms); only the alternating CO₂/H₂ transient exposes it. Notably absent from Fig. S20 (Cu–Ga/SiO₂): no CO* is detectable on the Ga-promoted catalyst at all, which the authors take as the direct cause of its 94% methanol selectivity — formate spillover to Ga³⁺ outruns formate decomposition on Cu, so the RWGS branch never opens.

bands.description: Linear (atop) CO carrying ¹³C instead of ¹²C — the same metal-surface stretch as ν(CO) linear (μ₁), red-shifted by roughly 45–50 cm⁻¹ by the heavier carbon. Substituting ¹³CO and watching a candidate band move by that predictable amount is the standard control for confirming a feature really is a CO stretch rather than a coincidental overlap, so this band exists mainly as the expected landing zone for that check. It also matters in its own right during ¹³CO₂ isotopic-transient work, where the shifted position is what the surface CO pool is actually tracked at.

references.note: Linear ¹³CO on Pt at the Pt–CeO₂ interface at 2005 cm⁻¹ under ¹³CO₂, against 2053 cm⁻¹ for the ¹²CO form on the same sites — a 48 cm⁻¹ shift, matching the expected value for a linear CO stretch and confirming the assignment.

bands.description: Bridging CO coordinated between two metal atoms. Lower frequency than linear CO due to increased metal→CO π-backdonation from the extra metal center, and typically broader/weaker than the linear band, often appearing as a shoulder below it rather than a fully separate peak. Usually emerges or grows in only at higher CO coverage, since it needs two adjacent free metal sites to form.

references.note: Ill-resolved bands below 2000 cm⁻¹ on Co/Al₂O₃ attributed to bridged and multibonded CO (Fig. 5a, Section 3.3); not separately resolved from the dominant linear CO band at 2041 cm⁻¹. Appear as a broad shoulder below the linear CO feature.

DFT-calculated (scaled) frequency of bridge-bound CO at the edges of Pd nanoparticles, growing from ~1886 cm⁻¹ for an isolated bridge CO up to ~1989 cm⁻¹ once the edge bridge sites are fully occupied by coadsorbed CO (Table 1) — matching the experimentally observed 1980–1990 cm⁻¹ band and implying particles ≥3 nm to host the necessary 10–12-CO edge ensemble.
Bridge-bound (Cu⁰)₂-CO (Fig. 3a; −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum).

bands.description: Three-fold hollow CO coordinated to three metal atoms at once. Stronger multi-center π-backdonation shifts ν(CO) well below both bridge and linear adsorption. Generally needs a close-packed facet to offer this coordination geometry at all, and tends to appear or strengthen with increasing coverage as simpler one- and two-fold sites fill up first.

references.note: DFT-calculated (scaled) frequencies of 3-fold hollow CO on Pd(111)-type facets/nanoparticles range from ~1802–1815 cm⁻¹ at low coverage up to ~1902 cm⁻¹ at the high-coverage (2×2)-3CO structure (0.75 ML), tracking the same coverage-dependent blue shift seen for bridge-bound CO.

bands.description: Four-fold hollow CO coordinated to four metal atoms at once — a comparatively rare coordination geometry, since it needs a specific square arrangement of surface atoms to form. Exhibits the lowest ν(CO) frequencies among metal-CO adsorption modes, since backdonation from four neighbors at once weakens the C-O bond more than any other coordination geometry.

Linear CO adsorbed on a Lewis-acidic cation site rather than a reduced metal atom. Markedly less metal→CO π-backdonation than on a metallic surface, blue-shifting ν(CO) above the free-gas value (2143 cm⁻¹) rather than below it — the opposite direction from every metallic-surface CO band in this dataset. Position correlates with the cation's formal charge and Lewis acidity, making this band a widely used spectroscopic probe of acid-site strength and oxidation state; the same ¹³CO isotope-shift check used for metallic sites applies here too.

references.note: New Cu⁺-CO feature appearing only after Ga loading (Fig. 3a; −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum); peak area scales with Ga₂O₃ content and correlates with TOF_MeOH — assigned to Cu⁺ at the Cu-Ga₂O₃ interface, the proposed methanol active site.

Monocarbonyl Cu⁺-CO in a Cu-exchanged zeolite, resolved by self-supporting-pellet transmission FTIR (100 K) into 4 distinct Cu⁺ site sub-families: 2166 cm⁻¹ (most electrophilic cationic site, preferentially covered by co-adsorbed H₂O), 2158 cm⁻¹ (principal/dominant cationic site), 2141 cm⁻¹ (a more highly-coordinated, oxide-like Cu⁺ site), and 2139 cm⁻¹ (Cu⁺(H₂O)(CO) mixed-ligand complex, nearly coincident with the oxide-like site). Site assignment supported by selective monocarbonyl→dicarbonyl→tricarbonyl conversion as CO coverage increases/temperature decreases — see co_gemdi_asym_2095/co_gemdi_sym_2035 for the dicarbonyl stage.

C-bonded (X⁺···CO) carbon monoxide on alkali-exchanged and protonic ZSM-5 zeolites (Si/Al = 14), assigned by transmission FTIR at 77 K. Position correlates linearly with 1/(R_M+R_CO)² (R_M = cation ionic radius), confirming a purely electrostatic, non-backdonating interaction — unlike the π-backdonating metallic-surface picture elsewhere in this dataset. High-frequency (HF) band positions at low CO coverage: Li⁺ 2188, Na⁺ 2178, K⁺ 2166, Rb⁺ 2162, Cs⁺ 2157, H⁺ (Brønsted) 2172 cm⁻¹ — frequency decreases monotonically with increasing cation radius/decreasing Lewis acidity. Each cation's HF band is accompanied by a much weaker low-frequency (LF) shoulder assigned to the O-bonded isomer of the same adduct, in thermodynamic equilibrium with this C-bonded form — see co_isocarbonyl_2220.

bands.description: Isocarbonyl species with CO coordinated through its oxygen end rather than carbon (M-OC) — the reverse orientation from every other CO-adsorption band in this dataset. On a purely electrostatic (non-backdonating) cation site, field-induced bond polarization runs opposite to C-bonding: O-bonding red-shifts ν(CO) below the free-gas value, paired with C-bonding's blue shift on the very same site, the two orientations coexisting as comparatively close-lying isomers in thermodynamic equilibrium rather than mutually exclusive species. Markedly weaker than the C-bonded band on the same site, since the C-bonded orientation is consistently the thermodynamically preferred one.

references.note: O-bonded (X⁺···OC) isocarbonyl species on the same alkali-exchanged and protonic ZSM-5 zeolites as co_cation_stretch_2175's HF band, in thermodynamic equilibrium with it: B3-LYP calculations on naked cations predict O-bonding is only slightly less stable than C-bonding, the energy gap narrowing from Li⁺ to Cs⁺, and a red-shifted shoulder consistent with that prediction is observed for every cation. Low-frequency (LF) band positions: Li⁺ 2108, Na⁺ 2113, K⁺ 2117, Rb⁺ 2119, Cs⁺ 2122, H⁺ (Brønsted) 2115 cm⁻¹ — frequency rises (shifts less below the free-gas 2143 cm⁻¹ value) with increasing cation radius, mirroring the HF band's opposite trend. Relative intensity of this band to the HF band (A_HF/A_LF) drops markedly from Li⁺ to Cs⁺, consistent with the two states' energies converging.

bands.description: Asymmetric ν(CO) component of a geminal dicarbonyl species: two linear CO ligands bound to a single isolated cationic metal center, stretching out of phase (one lengthens as the other shortens). The symmetric/asymmetric pair appearing together, rather than a single linear-CO band, is itself diagnostic of an atomically dispersed cationic site — a single metal atom isolated enough to bind two CO molecules at once. Typical splitting between the pair is ~50–60 cm⁻¹.

references.note: νₐₛ(CO) of Cu⁺(CO)₂ geminal dicarbonyl in a Cu-exchanged zeolite at 2151 cm⁻¹ (paired with νₛ at 2180, see co_gemdi_sym_2035), forming from the monocarbonyl with increasing CO coverage. The geminal (one-cation-two-CO) assignment was proven unambiguously by adsorbing a 1:1 ¹²CO+¹³CO isotopic mixture: a force-field calculation from the pure-¹²CO dicarbonyl frequencies predicted mixed-isotope Cu⁺(¹²CO)(¹³CO) bands at 2169/2113 cm⁻¹ and Cu⁺(¹³CO)₂ bands at 2131/2103 cm⁻¹, and both were observed exactly as calculated — only explainable if two CO ligands genuinely share one cation and vibrationally couple, ruling out two coincidentally-overlapping monocarbonyl bands from different sites.

bands.description: Symmetric ν(CO) component of geminal dicarbonyl species with two linear CO ligands bound to a single isolated cationic metal center. Appears together with the asymmetric band and is characteristic of isolated cationic adsorption sites.

references.note: νₛ(CO) of Cu⁺(CO)₂ geminal dicarbonyl in a Cu-exchanged zeolite at 2180 cm⁻¹ (paired with νₐₛ at 2151, see co_gemdi_asym_2095 for the ¹²CO/¹³CO isotopic-mixture proof of the geminal assignment). At low temperature, a further conversion to Cu⁺(CO)₃ tricarbonyl was observed (bands at 2190/2164/2140 cm⁻¹, not separately modeled in this dataset).

bands.description: Surface formyl C=O stretch (HCO*); mechanistic intermediate from CO + H. Often observed transiently. Distinguishes the CO-H pathway from formate-mediated routes.

references.note: Table 3, Fig. 3B (30 bar, 3H₂/CO₂, 513 K, Cu/ZnO in KBr): 1759 cm⁻¹; assigned to HCO* or weakly H-bonded *HCOOH (gaseous HCOOH at 1776 cm⁻¹). Intensity tracks methanol production rate — one of four GHSV-dependent bands (1759, 1691, 1457, 1398 cm⁻¹) identified as true intermediates; absent under 2H₂/CO.

bands.description: Formyl C-H stretch (HCO*); lower than formate ν(CH) at ~2870-2900 and weaker. Diagnostic when paired with C=O at ~1750.
Adsorbed formaldehyde C=O stretch (H₂CO*); reduction product of formyl. Key methanol precursor in some mechanisms.
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ asymmetric stretch (H₂CO*).
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ symmetric stretch (H₂CO*).
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ scissoring (H₂CO*); overlaps monodentate carbonate νₐₛ.
Generic surface acyl/aldehyde C=O stretch (R-C=O*); broad assignment used when species cannot be specifically identified. Distinguishes from formate by absence of ν(CH) at ~2870.
Hydroxymethyl O-H stretch (H₂COH*); late methanol precursor. Often masked by surface OH.
Hydroxymethyl CH₂ stretch (H₂COH*); overlaps methoxy and methanol.
Hydroxymethyl C-O stretch (H₂COH*); overlaps methoxy ν(C-O) at ~1050-1100.
Monodentate carbonate asymmetric stretch (m-CO₃²⁻*); small splitting (Δν ~100 cm⁻¹).

references.note: Table 3: νas(OCO⁻) at 1530 cm⁻¹; dominant CO₂ adsorption product on La-modified alumina; largely replaced by bidentate carbonate on active Ni-Ce-Fe/La-Al₂O₃.
Table 3, Fig. 3A (1 bar, 3H₂/CO₂, 513 K, Cu/ZnO in KBr): νₐₛ(OCO) monodentate carbonate (Fehr: 'unidentate') at 1464 cm⁻¹; Δν ≈ 64 cm⁻¹ vs. νₛ at 1400 cm⁻¹ confirms monodentate.

bands.description: Monodentate carbonate symmetric stretch (m-CO₃²⁻*).

references.note: Table 3: νₛ(-C-O) at 1340 cm⁻¹.
Table 3, Fig. 3 (3H₂/CO₂, 513 K, Cu/ZnO in KBr): νₛ(OCO) monodentate carbonate (Fehr: 'unidentate') at 1400 cm⁻¹ (1 bar) and 1398 cm⁻¹ (30 bar); paired with νₐₛ at 1464 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: Monodentate carbonate asymmetric stretch first overtone (m-CO₃²⁻*); rare but reported.

Bidentate carbonate asymmetric stretch (b-CO₃²⁻*); large splitting (Δν ~200–350 cm⁻¹). Position shifts with the base strength of the support: ~1510–1550 cm⁻¹ on less basic oxides (ZnO, CuO), ~1600–1670 cm⁻¹ on strongly basic ones (La₂O₃, CeO₂).

references.note: Table 3: νas(-C=O) 1670 + νas(OCO⁻) 1560 + νₛ(OCO⁻) 1500 cm⁻¹; dominant CO₂ activation product on active catalyst under DRM at 600°C; stabilised by surface oxygen vacancies.

Bidentate carbonate at 1605 cm⁻¹ confirmed as active RWGS intermediate by ¹³C isotopic exchange at 200°C: ¹³CO₂ replaces ¹²C faster than the formate pool, indicating these carbonates are directly involved in the catalytic cycle.

Table 3, Fig. 3A (3H₂/CO₂, 513 K, Cu/ZnO in KBr): νₐₛ(OCO) bidentate carbonate at 1543 cm⁻¹ (1 bar) and 1511 cm⁻¹ (30 bar); Δν = 224 cm⁻¹ vs. νₛ at 1319 cm⁻¹ confirms bidentate. Sits at the low-frequency end of the bidentate range — typical for ZnO/CuO supports vs. ~1600–1670 cm⁻¹ on more basic oxides.

Fig. 6a/S56d,e (CO₂/N₂ 20 vol%, 320°C, 20 bar): b-CO₃* disappears instantaneously on switching to H₂. Position shifts slightly with Zn loading: 1532 cm⁻¹ (30 mol%), 1523 cm⁻¹ (20 mol%), 1525 cm⁻¹ (90 mol%).
Fig. S56f (CO₂/N₂ 20 vol%, 320°C, 20 bar): carbonate adsorption on ZnO reference; weaker intensity than ZnHfOx, consistent with low CO₂ activation capacity of ZnO.

bands.description: Bidentate carbonate symmetric stretch (b-CO₃²⁻*).

references.note: Table 3: νₛ(-C-O) at 1310 cm⁻¹; paired with the asymmetric modes at 1670/1560/1500 cm⁻¹.
Bidentate carbonate symmetric stretch at 1251 cm⁻¹; paired with ν_as at 1605 cm⁻¹ (Δν ≈ 354 cm⁻¹ consistent with bidentate coordination). ¹³C exchange confirms activity in RWGS.
Table 3, Fig. 3A (1 bar, 3H₂/CO₂, 513 K, Cu/ZnO in KBr): νₛ(OCO) bidentate carbonate at 1319 cm⁻¹; paired with νₐₛ at 1543 cm⁻¹ (Δν = 224 cm⁻¹ confirms bidentate).
Fig. 6a (CO₂/N₂ 20 vol%, 320°C, 20 bar): b-CO₃* νₛ(OCO); disappears instantaneously on switching to H₂.
Fig. S56f (CO₂/N₂ 20 vol%, 320°C, 20 bar): carbonate νₛ on ZnO reference.

bands.description: Bidentate carbonate ν₂ in-phase symmetric stretch of the two surface-bound C-O bonds (b-CO₃²⁻*): both surface-bonded oxygens expand and contract in unison while the free terminal oxygen counter-moves slightly. Lower-frequency member of the split degenerate pair (the out-of-phase counterpart is νₐₛ(OCO) at ~1500–1670 cm⁻¹). Rarely reported separately from the higher-frequency modes because it falls in a region also occupied by methoxy ν(CO) and formaldehyde bands.

Fig. 4a/4c and Figs. S16/S19/S20 (operando DRIFTS, 230 °C, 10–20 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 3, Cu–M/SiO₂ from SOMC): ν(C–H) of κ²-HCOO* bound to the isolated cationic promoter, resolved by MCR-ALS as a component kinetically distinct from κ²-HCOO*(Cu⁰) at 2850–2860 cm⁻¹. bands.description: Formate C-H stretch of κ²-HCOO* bound to a metallic Cu surface, sitting some 20–40 cm⁻¹ below the same mode on a cationic or oxide site (see ν(CH) HCOO* above) — the split is large enough to tell the two formate populations apart in one spectrum, which is what makes Cu-vs-promoter formate spillover observable at all. Two traps at this position: methoxy's νₛ(CH₃) on silica lands within a few cm⁻¹ of it, and adsorbed methanol's νₛ(CH₃) is close too, so a band here is only safely formate once its partner combination band near 2930 cm⁻¹ (or a deuteration/MCR check) backs it up.

references.note: Fig. 4a/4c (time-resolved and steady-state, 2856 cm⁻¹), Fig. 5b (MCR-resolved, 2850 cm⁻¹) and Fig. 7a (2850/2854 cm⁻¹) — operando DRIFTS, 230 °C, 10–20 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 3. The first and most abundant surface species over all four catalysts (Cu/SiO₂, Cu–Zn/SiO₂, Cu–Ga/SiO₂, Cu–In/SiO₂). MCR-resolved per catalyst in the SI: Fig. S15 2860 and Fig. S18 2852 cm⁻¹ (Cu/SiO₂), Fig. S16 2850 and Fig. S20 2848 cm⁻¹ (Cu–Ga/SiO₂), Fig. S17 2858 and Fig. S19 2854 cm⁻¹ (Cu–In/SiO₂); Fig. S10 shows the same feature dominating all four time-resolved spectra from the first minutes onward. Exchanges to κ²-DCOO* within the 10 s spectral acquisition limit under D₂, so formate formation and exchange are not rate-limiting. On Cu it is also the RWGS intermediate: its decay tracks the rise of CO* at 2108–2115 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: Formate asymmetric OCO stretch (HCOO*) — the key HCOO* marker band, since this in-phase/antiphase C-O stretch pair (paired with νₛ(OCO) below) is a clean fingerprint distinct from carbonate or carboxylate features. Usually the more intense of the two paired stretches, and the easier one to spot first in a spectrum. Its exact position isn't a single fixed value — it shifts with the underlying adsorption geometry, so it's always worth cross-checking against the symmetric partner band and the Δν splitting between them (itself a geometry diagnostic, see νₛ(OCO) below) rather than relying on this band's position alone.

references.note: Table 2/Fig. 1a (Ru/Al₂O₃) and Fig. 3a (Ru–6.1%"Na₂O"/Al₂O₃ DFM): νas(OCO) HCOO* at 1520 cm⁻¹ on both surfaces, appearing at the onset of H₂ reduction (methanation step, 320 °C, 20% H₂/N₂). On Ru/Al₂O₃, formate forms via spillover of bicarbonates (adsorbed on Al₂O₃ OH groups); on Ru–Na₂O/Al₂O₃, it forms after bidentate carbonates (on Al-O⁻-Na⁺ sites) spill over to the Ru–support interface — same position despite the different CO₂ adsorption pathway. Confirmed reaction intermediate en route to CH₄.

νas(OCO) at 1600 cm⁻¹ (ME-DRIFTS, 20 bar, 260°C); confirmed active intermediate by CO₂ modulation-excitation PSD — responds at same frequency as product formation. Also at 1590 cm⁻¹ during methanol steam reforming on Cu-GaZrOx-24.
Table 3: νas(OCO⁻) at 1585 cm⁻¹; dominant CH₄ adsorption product on Al₂O₃ via H-abstraction; nearly absent on La-modified and Ni-Ce-Fe/La-Al₂O₃ under DRM.

On Fe₃O₄(001) (Fig. 6c): two bidentate-bridging components, 1555 cm⁻¹ (tet site: oct-Fe above tet-Fe beneath) and 1548/1538 cm⁻¹ (p/s-pol; int site: oct-Fe above interstitial Fe) — paired νₛ(OCO) at 1369/1377 cm⁻¹ (tet/int); distinction only possible with polarized light due to Fano overlap in unpolarized spectra. On Fe₃O₄(111) (Fig. 6b/d): quasi-bidentate at 1588 cm⁻¹ (one O to Fe-tet, other to surface OH; paired νₛ at 1335 cm⁻¹, positive inverted Fano sign — TDM parallel to surface) and chelating at 1548 cm⁻¹ very weak (both O to single Fe-tet; paired νₛ at 1380 cm⁻¹); bidentate-bridging excluded here (Fe-tet neighbor distance 5.9 Å too large). Chelating forms first (from 0.05 L); quasi-bidentate develops above 0.2 L.

Table 3, Fig. 3 (3H₂/CO₂, 513 K, Cu/ZnO in KBr): νₐₛ(OCO) formate at 1587 cm⁻¹ (1 bar) and 1603 cm⁻¹ (30 bar). Both show large Δν (~230–290 cm⁻¹ vs. νₛ at 1360/1314 cm⁻¹) consistent with bidentate binding — Fehr's 'unidentate' label for the 30-bar species contradicts the Δν. Spectroscopically prominent surface spectator: intensity independent of GHSV, persists on inactive CZ_2000.

Fig. 6b (H₂/N₂ 80 vol%, 320°C, 20 bar): HCOO* ν(C=O) forms instantaneously on switching from CO₂ to H₂; intensity decreases as methoxy builds up, consistent with active intermediate in the formate-methoxy pathway.

Fig. 7a (MCR-resolved, He+CO₂ vs H₂+He switching, 230 °C, 20 bar, Cu–Zn/SiO₂): νₐₛ(C–O) of κ²-HCOO* at 1590 cm⁻¹, resolved alongside the same component's ν(C–H) at 2850 cm⁻¹ so the C–H and C–O regions can be cross-checked against one MCR component rather than assigned separately. Fig. S19 in the SI gives 1544 cm⁻¹ for the same species on Cu–In/SiO₂ — some 46 cm⁻¹ lower, the same direction the promoter shifts every other formate band here. Fig. 6a plots this frequency (for the deuterated κ²-DCOO* form) against intrinsic CH₃OH formation rate as a Sabatier volcano spanning roughly 1530–1600 cm⁻¹ across the four catalysts, weaker C–O binding on the right; the per-catalyst values behind that plot are not tabulated.

bands.description: Formate symmetric OCO stretch (HCOO*), paired with νₐₛ(OCO) above. The splitting Δν = νₐₛ − νₛ between the two paired bands is a standard diagnostic for adsorption geometry — how it compares between a more bridging-like and a more chelating-like coordination is a recurring theme in formate vibrational assignments. Where multiple coordination geometries coexist and overlap, polarization-dependent IRRAS/DRIFTS can resolve components that look like a single broad feature in an unpolarized spectrum.

references.note: Table 2/Fig. 1a (Ru/Al₂O₃) and Fig. 3a (Ru–6.1%"Na₂O"/Al₂O₃ DFM): νₛ(OCO) HCOO* at 1320 cm⁻¹ on both surfaces, paired with νas at 1520 cm⁻¹; appears at onset of H₂ reduction (320 °C, 20% H₂/N₂). On Ru/Al₂O₃, formate forms via bicarbonate spillover at the Ru–Al₂O₃ interface; on Ru–Na₂O/Al₂O₃, from bidentate carbonate spillover to the Ru–support interface. Identified as a key CO₂ methanation intermediate.

Table 1, Fig. 6a–d: νₛ(OCO) of bidentate HCOO* resolved by p-polarized IRRAS (negative Fano profiles, TDM perpendicular to surface; dissociative HCOOH adsorption, room temperature, UHV). On Fe₃O₄(001) (Fig. 6a/c): bidentate-bridging, two components — 1369 cm⁻¹ (tet site) and 1377 cm⁻¹ (int site), Epn coupling; paired νas(OCO) at 1555/1548 cm⁻¹ (tet/int); δ(CH) at 1373/1385 cm⁻¹ also observed with inverted Fano shape. On Fe₃O₄(111) (Fig. 6b/d): quasi-bidentate at 1335 cm⁻¹ (paired νas at 1588 cm⁻¹) and chelating at 1380 cm⁻¹ (paired νas at 1548 cm⁻¹); no bidentate-bridging here (Fe-tet spacing 5.9 Å too large). Chelating forms first (from 0.05 L); quasi-bidentate develops above 0.2 L.

Table 3, Fig. 3B (30 bar, 3H₂/CO₂, 513 K, Cu/ZnO in KBr): δ(CH) formate at 1371 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: Formate combination band (HCOO*): bending + asymmetric stretch; diagnostic for HCOO*. Runs low enough on cationic-promoted Cu (~2923 cm⁻¹) to sit right on top of methoxy νₐₛ(CH₃) — the two are told apart by deuteration, which moves this combination out of the C-H region altogether while methoxy's own fundamental simply shifts down to its C-D position.

references.note: Formate combination band on Cu⁺ at Cu–Ga₂O₃.

Upper arm of the formate ν(CH) Fermi resonance doublet at 2945 cm⁻¹ on CeO₂ (lower arm at 2910 cm⁻¹). The ~35 cm⁻¹ doublet splitting is characteristic of HCOO* Fermi coupling between ν(CH) and 2δ(CH) or δ(OCH)+νₐₛ(OCO).

Deuteration is what proves the combination character: under D₂ this feature leaves the C–H region entirely, while the genuine ν(C–D) fundamental appears at 2161–2184 cm⁻¹, which is precisely why the SSITKA C–D window is the clean one for reading out formate bond strengths.

bands.description: Formate higher combination band (HCOO*); sometimes assigned as 2ν(C=O) overtone in older literature.

C-D stretch of κ²-DCOO* on metallic Cu — the deuterated counterpart of ν(CH) HCOO*(Cu⁰) at ~2856 cm⁻¹, red-shifted by the ~0.73 harmonic-oscillator mass factor. Its position across a promoter series is a direct readout of formate C-H(D) bond strength, which in turn tracks how readily the formate decomposes to CO rather than being hydrogenated on: stronger C-D, less decomposition, higher methanol selectivity. Sits on top of gas-phase CO's R branch and, at the low end, of the deuterated-methoxy region, so a gas-phase subtraction (or a component-resolved analysis) is needed before reading a position off it.

references.note: Fig. 5b (MCR-resolved, Cu–Zn/SiO₂ SSITKA, CO₂+D₂ ⇄ CO₂+H₂, 230 °C, 10 bar, H₂ or D₂/CO₂ = 3): κ²-DCOO*(Cu) at 2167 cm⁻¹. Per catalyst in the SI: Fig. S15 2161 cm⁻¹ (Cu/SiO₂), Fig. S16 2176 cm⁻¹ (Cu–Ga/SiO₂), Fig. S17 2169 cm⁻¹ (Cu–In/SiO₂). Fig. 6b plots those four points and uses 2173 cm⁻¹ for Cu–Zn/SiO₂ — the Gaussian-fitted centre of the overlapping Cu⁰ and Zn²⁺ components, not a separate species; across Cu/SiO₂ → Cu–In → Cu–Zn → Cu–Ga the ν(C–D) frequency rises monotonically and intrinsic CH₃OH selectivity rises linearly with it (R² > 0.99), making this band a quantitative selectivity descriptor. SI section 1.5.5 derives the expected ν(C–D)/ν(C–H) ratio of ≈0.734 from the harmonic-oscillator reduced masses and uses it to assign this region; Fig. S14 shows the exchange with κ²-HCOO* completes in under 1 min at both switches, so the kinetic isotope effect on formate hydrogenation is negligible.

bands.description: C-D stretch of κ²-DCOO* bound to a cationic promoter site rather than to metallic Cu, ~17 cm⁻¹ above its Cu-bound counterpart — the deuterated echo of the same Cu⁰-vs-cation split seen in the C-H region, and the cleanest single piece of evidence that formate genuinely occupies two distinct sites at once rather than one averaged environment. Only resolvable where the promoter's own formate is spectroscopically separable in the first place.

references.note: Fig. 5b (MCR-resolved, Cu–Zn/SiO₂ SSITKA, CO₂+D₂ ⇄ CO₂+H₂, 230 °C, 10 bar): κ²-DCOO*(Zn²⁺) at 2184 cm⁻¹, kinetically indistinguishable from κ²-DCOO*(Cu) at 2167 cm⁻¹ but spectrally separate — direct evidence that Zn²⁺ supplies a second, distinct Lewis-acid site for formate and simultaneously perturbs the formate on the adjacent Cu. Not resolved for Ga³⁺ or In³⁺ in this region (Figs. S16/S17), where the promoter-bound component overlaps κ²-DCOO*(Cu) or is too dilute at steady state.

bands.description: Methoxy CH₃ asymmetric stretch (CH₃O*) — one C-H bond stretching out of phase with the other two. Position shifts with adsorption site/coordination environment, tracking together with νₛ(CH₃) below, so a shift in this band is a useful sign that the binding environment itself has changed. A coadsorbed methanol band sits close by, a little higher in frequency, so the two are worth distinguishing carefully rather than assuming a single species. Silica is the outlier among supports: methoxy grafted to SiO₂ as Si-O-CH₃ absorbs near the top of the range (~2955–2960 cm⁻¹), some 30 cm⁻¹ above the same mode on Cu and well clear of the more usual oxide values.

references.note: Monodentate CH₃O* from CH₃OH dosing on anatase TiO₂.
ν_as(CH₃) on Cu⁺ at Cu–Ga₂O₃; downshifted from ~2926 cm⁻¹ on unpromoted Cu/SiO₂ — diagnostic of the Ga promoter-induced site change.
ν_as(CH₃) at 2970 cm⁻¹ on Zr⁴⁺ sites of Zr-rich CuGaZrOx.
Fig. 6b (H₂/N₂ 80 vol%, 320°C, 20 bar): νₐₛ(CH₃) H₃CO*; forms as formate is hydrogenated in the formate-methoxy pathway.

Fig. 4a/4c (2958 cm⁻¹) and Fig. 7a (2956 cm⁻¹) — operando DRIFTS, 230 °C, 10–20 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 3, Cu–M/SiO₂ from SOMC; MCR-resolved per catalyst in the SI at Fig. S15 2956, Fig. S16 2958, Fig. S18 2952, Fig. S20 2958 cm⁻¹. Methoxy grafted to the silica support (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or to the promoter: it builds up slowly (visible only after ~90 min) and, unlike formate, exchanges on the minute-to-hour timescale under D₂. Fig. S14 splits it into a fast, reactive pool near the Cu/promoter interface and a slow (τ ≈ 1 h) spectator pool on remote silica sites — one band, two kinetically distinct populations. The reactive pool's hydrogenation/desorption is the rate-limiting step of the whole cycle (KIE = 2.78), which makes this band a rate proxy rather than a spectator.

bands.description: Methoxy CH₃ symmetric stretch (CH₃O*), shifting in tandem with νₐₛ(CH₃) above. Often appears as a close shoulder pair with a coadsorbed methanol band sitting a little higher in frequency. Silica-grafted methoxy is the extreme case, ~2856–2859 cm⁻¹, some 40 cm⁻¹ above the same mode on Cu — high enough that it lands directly on formate's own ν(CH) on metallic Cu (see ν(CH) HCOO*(Cu⁰)). On a silica-supported Cu catalyst the two are effectively coincident and cannot be separated by position alone.

references.note: ν_s(CH₃) on Cu⁺ at Cu–Ga₂O₃; downshifted from ~2842 cm⁻¹ on unpromoted Cu/SiO₂ — mirrors the ν_as(CH₃) site-diagnostic shift.
ν_s(CH₃) at 2819 cm⁻¹ on Zr⁴⁺ sites of Zr-rich CuGaZrOx.

Fig. 6b/S49/S56 (H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1, 320°C, 20 bar): νₛ(CH₃) H₃CO* used as key tracker band; ~2827 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOx, ~2832 cm⁻¹ (20ZnHfOx), ~2834 cm⁻¹ (90ZnHfOx). On ZnO: 2825 cm⁻¹, only very weak bands (poor methoxy formation from CO₂ on pure ZnO).

Fig. 4a/4c (2858 cm⁻¹) and Fig. 7a (2854 cm⁻¹) — operando DRIFTS, 230 °C, 10–20 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 3, Cu–M/SiO₂ from SOMC; MCR-resolved per catalyst in the SI at Fig. S15 2856, Fig. S16 2858, Fig. S17 2856, Fig. S18 2859, Fig. S20 2858 cm⁻¹. Under D₂ this fundamental shifts cleanly to 2080 cm⁻¹ (CD₃O*), which is what allows methoxy to be separated from the formate combination band it otherwise overlaps in the C-H region.

bands.description: Methoxy CH₃ symmetric deformation (CH₃O*) — the methyl "umbrella" mode. Usually the only CH₃-deformation-region band resolved at all, since it's the sole totally-symmetric (A₁) one and therefore the only one with a surface-normal dipole derivative on an ideally perpendicular adsorbate; on real, less rigidly-oriented oxide-supported catalysts it can be unusually weak. Position is comparatively insensitive to binding geometry, unlike the stretches above.

references.note: Table 3: δ(–CH₃) at 1480 cm⁻¹; surface methoxy deformation from CH₄ activation via H-abstraction; observed during DRM at 600°C.
Table 3, Fig. 3B (30 bar, 3H₂/CO₂, 513 K, Cu/ZnO in KBr): δ(CH₃) methoxy at 1457 cm⁻¹; intensity tracks GC methanol production rate — GHSV-dependent, absent under 2H₂/CO.

bands.description: Tentatively assigned methoxy CH₃ asymmetric deformation (CH₃O*). Not always separately resolved from δₛ(CH₃) above — some spectra show only the symmetric component. May overlap with formate νₛ(OCO) at ~1365 cm⁻¹, so a band here doesn't necessarily rule out formate also being present.

Monodentate methoxy C-O stretch (CH₃O* bonded via O to a single metal cation). Often resolves into several closely-spaced sub-components rather than one clean peak, reflecting a distribution of slightly different monodentate sites rather than a single uniform one. Diagnostic threshold: ν(C-O) above roughly 1100 cm⁻¹ indicates monodentate geometry, below it bidentate (see methoxy_co_stretch_bi_1045) — the two share the same underlying vibration and just trade off in relative position with coordination number.

references.note: Sub-components at 1100/1126/1156 cm⁻¹ reflecting a distribution of monodentate sites; dominates over bidentate ~3:1 by integrated area; ~1.5× higher photoreactivity toward HCOO* than bidentate.
Zr-OCH₃ species: methoxy coordinated to Zr⁴⁺ sites on CuGaZrOx at 1152 cm⁻¹.

Fig. 6b (H₂/N₂ 80 vol%, 320°C, 20 bar): terminal methoxy (t-H₃CO*) ν(CO); forms as formate is hydrogenated. Assigned as terminal based on position above 1100 cm⁻¹; paired with bridged methoxy at 1052 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: Bidentate methoxy C-O stretch (CH₃O* bridging two metal centers, or bonded at a bridging-O vacancy). Diagnostic threshold: ν(C-O) below roughly 1100 cm⁻¹ indicates bidentate geometry (see methoxy_co_stretch_mono_1130 for the monodentate counterpart). Overlaps closely with molecular methanol's own ν(C-O) — distinguish via the absence of methanol's own νₛ(CH₃) marker band at higher frequency.

references.note: Similar thermal stability to monodentate (no interconversion ≤ 300 °C); ~1.5× lower photoreactivity toward HCOO* than monodentate.
Fig. 6b (H₂/N₂ 80 vol%, 320°C, 20 bar): bridged methoxy (b-H₃CO*) ν(CO); consistent with CH₃O* at a Zn–V_O–Hf oxygen-vacancy site. Paired with terminal methoxy at 1153 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: CD₃ symmetric stretch of deuterated methoxy — the deuterated counterpart of νₛ(CH₃) CH₃O*, and the only methoxy band that survives deuteration as a cleanly resolvable feature. That makes it unusually valuable: in the ordinary C-H region methoxy overlaps both formate's combination band and adsorbed methanol, whereas here it sits ~80 cm⁻¹ clear of the deuterated formate bands and can be integrated on its own. Practically the price is a crowded neighbourhood of a different kind, since this is also where CO on reduced metals and CO₂'s own combination bands absorb.

references.note: Fig. 5b/5c (MCR-resolved, Cu–Zn/SiO₂ SSITKA, CO₂+D₂ ⇄ CO₂+H₂, 230 °C, 10 bar): CD₃O* on silica at 2080 cm⁻¹, and at exactly the same position on the other three catalysts (SI Figs. S15/S16/S17) — unshifted by the promoter, consistent with methoxy sitting on the silica support rather than at the Cu–promoter interface. Unlike formate, this exchanges slowly, and its concentration profile — not the formate's — tracks the delayed appearance of gas-phase methanol, which is the observation that identifies methoxy hydrogenation/desorption as the rate-limiting step. Fig. S14c/d resolves the decay into a fast reactive pool (τ ≈ 1–6 min) and a slow spectator pool (τ ≈ 55–98 min); Fig. S12 is the linearised fit behind the KIE of 2.78. The asymmetric νₐₛ(C–D) partner is expected near 2160 cm⁻¹ and is not resolved, being buried under κ²-DCOO*.

bands.description: Methanol O-H stretch (MeOH*/MeOH(g)) — broad and hydrogen-bonding-sensitive like most O-H stretches, so its exact shape depends heavily on the local hydrogen-bonding environment. Often obscured by adsorbed water and surface hydroxyl groups absorbing in the same broad region.

references.note: Table I (CH₃OH vapor): ν(OH) Q 3687 cm⁻¹ (vs); R 3713, P 3673; collapses to ~3337 cm⁻¹, very strong and broad, in the liquid due to H-bonding. The CH₃OD counterpart from the same paper's Table II is filed separately — see ν(OD) CH₃OD.

bands.description: O-D stretch of O-deuterated methanol, the hydroxyl counterpart of ν(OH) MeOH nearly 1000 cm⁻¹ lower. Deliberately drawn as the full R-to-P envelope rather than the Q branch alone, since all three branches sit inside 40 cm⁻¹. The practical value of knowing where it lands is negative rather than positive: methanol's O-H stretch is the band most easily lost under support hydroxyls and adsorbed water, and moving it here is one of the few ways to get it out of that region — but the new position then collides with the C-H stretching region instead, so the escape is only partial.

bands.description: Adsorbed methanol CH₃ asymmetric stretch (CH₃OH*). Typically blue-shifted ~10–20 cm⁻¹ relative to methoxy νₐₛ(CH₃); the cleanest C-H region marker to distinguish molecularly-adsorbed methanol from methoxy. In the isolated gas-phase molecule this region is strongly resonance-mixed with overtones/combinations of the δCH₃ modes (see the vibration-modes page) rather than a single clean fundamental — worth keeping in mind even though that fine structure washes out on a real catalyst surface.

bands.description: Sharp, narrow O-H stretch from an isolated terminal hydroxyl group — not hydrogen-bonded to a neighbor, which is exactly why it stays sharp rather than broadening the way the H-bonded band below does.
Broader band; bridged or hydrogen-bonded hydroxyls.

Gas-phase water symmetric O-H stretch (ν₁, A₁) — both O-H bonds lengthening and shortening together, in phase. Sharp and well-resolved in the gas phase, in contrast to the broad, merged envelope this band collapses into once adsorbed/condensed (see h2o_stretch_3400).
Gas-phase water H-O-H angle bend (ν₂, A₁) — the only bending mode this 3-atom molecule has. The strongest of the three gas-phase fundamentals.

Gas-phase water asymmetric O-H stretch (ν₃, B₂) — one O-H bond lengthening while the other shortens, out of phase. Sits just above the symmetric stretch, and the two are usually only cleanly resolved in the gas phase.

Gallium hydride (Ga-H*) stretch — a marker for heterolytic H₂ dissociation across a Lewis acid/base pair. Confirmed by substituting D₂ for H₂: the band red-shifts by the mass-dependent amount expected for a genuine M-H(D) stretch, ruling out a coincidental overlap with something else. Can play a role in surface hydrogen-transfer chemistry, e.g. converting a formate-type species toward a methoxy-type one via H spillover.

references.note: Ga-H at 1976 cm⁻¹; confirmed by D₂ substitution (isotope shift observed). Present on GaZrOx and CuGaZrOx under CO₂/H₂ at 20 bar, 260°C. Partially static during MES — consistent with slow HCOO* → CH₃O* conversion.
